transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Janine Herbst.
Stephen Miller takes over as White House Chief of Staff Monday, replacing Suzy Wiles.
NPR's Windsor Johnston reports President Trump announced the move just days after Republicans
suffered major midterm losses.
Democrats are sharply criticizing Miller's promotion as they prepared to take control
of Congress.
Virginia Congressman Don Beyer reacted to the news during an interview with the BBC.
Stephen Miller is probably the single darkest force, the Darth Vader of this country right
now, of this presidential leadership.
What he's done with the cruel and chaotic immigration enforcement.
President Trump praised Miller at an event in Florida last night.
He's very loyal, smart, he does a great job.
He's been an MVP every year.
Miller has been with Trump since the 2016 presidential campaign.
He moves up from Deputy Chief of Staff while Wiles shifts to the administration's political
operation.
Windsor Johnston, NPR News, Washington.
A new Democratic-led House and Senate comes in in January, but first, the current Congress
has some business to take care of, including a looming possible federal government shutdown
in December when a stopgap funding bill expires.
Here's Eric McDaniel has more.
Government funding that runs out of money in December 11th, so just about a month away.
They're also not going to negotiate the full suite of 12 annual spending bills, so they'll
do some kind of kick the can extension and Democrats will have to deal with it in the
new Congress.
Still, it's going to be messy.
I should also say that it's almost certain we'll see a vote this week to impeach the
Secretary of Defense, who's upset even enough Republican lawmakers over his lack of transparency
about the war in Iran to make that vote pretty interesting to watch.
This is an effort that was first brought by Republican Thomas Massey of Kentucky.
And here's Eric McDaniel reporting.
This year's El Nino could be the strongest on record.
The natural climate pattern shifts weather across the globe.
Areas across the U.S. have already felt impacts, and it's driving an El Nino economy.
And here's Eva Berger reports.
Drainage contractors are very popular in California right now.
Jim Garner, who owns a construction company, says he's booked four months in advance.
In fact, it's to the point where I can barely keep up with it.
California has already seen some of El Nino's impacts, higher sea level, greater chance
for coastal flooding.
But it's not just California that will see different weather this year.
Across the country, warmer and wetter conditions are forecasted for most of the continental
U.S.
So a range of companies are either preparing to or are already seeing a bump in business.
We're talking tire sellers, ski mountains, and mold-sniffing dogs.
That's not a group that typically has something in common.
Thanks to El Nino, now they do.
Eva Berger, NPR News.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
Airlines, airports, and broadcasters across Europe are bracing for more hoax bomb threats
following a week of flight disruptions and evacuations.
Vicki Barker reports from London that investigators are trying to determine who's responsible
and whether the threats are connected.
National and regional investigators are trying to find out who's behind the hoaxes, which
have come amid a backdrop of cyber attacks and drone sightings apparently designed to
disrupt civilian infrastructure and daily life.
More than two dozen commercial flights between 16 countries were targeted over two days this
past week.
London's Heathrow Airport and Birmingham's airport also received threats.
Then, on Friday, several media organizations in Ireland, Bulgaria, and the U.K. were forced
to evacuate after emails warned of bombs in their buildings.
But whether this represented an escalation by the original hoaxers or was the work of
separate actors isn't yet clear.
For NPR News, I'm Vicki Barker in London.
Democratic Senator Chris Murphy of Connecticut has been discharged from the hospital after
suffering a stroke.
He says he will miss several weeks of Senate votes as he recovers in a rehab center.
The 53-year-old says doctors told him he had a small hemorrhagic stroke and that they expect
him to make a full recovery.
Murphy, who serves on the Appropriations Committee and is a leading voice on immigration and
gun policy, is among those considered as a potential 2028 presidential candidate.
This is NPR News.

topics.text: Stephen Miller takes over as White House Chief of Staff, replacing Suzy Wiles after GOP midterm losses
Democrats criticize Miller's promotion; Rep. Don Beyer calls him the Darth Vader of the administration
Congress faces possible federal government shutdown December 11 when stopgap funding expires
Impeachment vote expected this week against Defense Secretary over lack of transparency on Iran war
Strong El Niño expected to reshape U.S. weather, boosting drainage, tire, and ski businesses in California
European airports and airlines face hoax bomb threats after week of flight disruptions and evacuations
Hoax bomb threats force evacuation of media organizations in Ireland, Bulgaria, and the U.K.
Sen. Chris Murphy discharged from hospital after small hemorrhagic stroke, expects full recovery
